Sign in to your Collider account Add Us Add on Google Preferred Source Google News Summary Generate a summary of this story Like Like follow Follow followed Followed Listen Thread Log in Here is a fact-based summary of the story contents: Try something different: Show me the facts Explain it like I’m 5 Give me a lighthearted recap The thriller genre has a pretty standard formula. There is a mystery, the tension builds, and everything leads to one major reveal. The structure works for a reason, and plenty of great shows have used it successfully in many different ways. However, the more interesting thrillers are the ones that move beyond those boundaries. Of course, taking an unconventional approach does not always guarantee mainstream success. Some of the most compelling thriller shows are unfortunately drowned out simply because they were released at the wrong time or were too unusual to attract a big audience. However, that doesn’t mean they deserve any less appreciation. Here are six such miniseries that you probably haven’t seen, but are worth every second. 6 ‘A Spy Among Friends’ (2022) Damian Lewis starring ahead in A Spy Among Friends Image via MGM+ A Spy Among Friends , based on Ben Macintyre’s nonfiction book, does not unfold like the typical spy thriller. The six-part miniseries follows MI6 officer Nicholas Elliott ( Damian Lewis ) and his close friend Kim Philby ( Guy Pearce ), who happens to be one of the most destructive Soviet double agents in British history. When the story begins, the audience already knows Philby is a traitor. The question is how he managed to deceive Britain, America, and Elliott for so long. The show opens in 1963, with Elliott traveling to Beirut and confronting Philby about his years of spying for the Soviet Union. He hopes to extract a confession and bring his old friend home, but Philby soon escapes to Moscow. Back in Britain, Elliott is questioned by MI5 officer Lily Thomas (Anna Maxwell Martin), who suspects that he might be hiding something. Their tense conversations form the backbone of the series as it moves between the interrogation, Beirut, and earlier periods in Elliott and Philby’s friendship. A Spy Among Friends does not feature fancy gadgets, constant action, and high-octane missions. The show taps into the psychology of espionage by focusing on how deeply Phil understood the people around him to be able to fool them. The six-episode structure is paced almost perfectly. Each shift in time reveals just enough to change the meaning of the interrogation without overwhelming the audience. The series takes its time to reveal the truth, but every single conversation builds up to an unforgettable finale that does perfect justice to this compelling narrative. 5 ‘Station Eleven’ (2021–2022) MacKenzie Davis reading the Station Eleven comic book in a rainy tent in Station Eleven. Image via HBO Max Station Eleven is a 10-part sci-fi miniseries set 20 years after most of humanity has disappeared and follows a group of actors who travel around Lake Michigan performing Shakespeare for scattered communities of survivors. That sounds like the exact opposite of the sci-fi genre, but that’s the entire point of the show. The story begins during a production of King Lear in Chicago, where famous actor Arthur Leander ( Gael García Bernal ) suddenly collapses onstage. Jeevan Chaudhary ( Himesh Patel ), an audience member with no real idea what he is doing, rushes forward to help. He later finds himself looking after eight-year-old cast member Kirsten Raymonde (Matilda Lawler) just as news begins spreading about a deadly flu. The pair take shelter with Jeevan’s brother, Frank (Nabhaan Rizwan) , while the city outside them quickly falls apart. Two decades later, Kirsten is played by Mackenzie Davis and has become a fiercely protective member of the troupe called Traveling Symphony. However, their routine performances are interrupted by the arrival of a mysterious man known as the Prophet (Daniel Zovatto), whose connection to Kirsten, Arthur, and a rare graphic novel titled Station Eleven gradually brings the show’s different timelines together. The series keeps moving between the world before the pandemic, the terrifying weeks immediately after it, and the strange new society built from what remains. That structure can feel disorienting at first, but the pieces eventually connect in ways that give the show its emotional weight. Although the show premiered at a time when most audiences had no interest in watching a pandemic story, it managed to take a completely different approach to it. That’s because instead of simply being another survival story, Station Eleven focused on human beings’ relentless search for meaning in the wake of absolute devastation. 4 ‘True Story’ (2021) True Story Netflix Wesley Snipes Kevin Hart Image via Netflix True Story , created by Eric Newman , is a seven-part Netflix miniseries starring Kevin Hart as world-famous comedian Kid, whose life comes crashing down when he reunites with his reckless old brother ( Wesley Snipes ) for a night out during a tour stop in his hometown. Kid wakes the next morning beside a dead woman with no memory of what happened. Now, Carlton insists that involving the police would destroy everything he has built, so the brothers attempt to deal with the situation, but every decision creates a more dangerous problem. Soon enough, Kid is being blackmailed, violent men are asking questions, and an obsessive fan named Gene (Theo Rossi) becomes involved at the worst possible moment. The show doesn’t really hinge on solving the mystery about this dead woman, but more so on how far Kid is willing to go to protect his career and reputation. The series has a meta quality to it thanks to the similarities between Kid and Hart’s own public image. Not just that, but the comedian also does a great job in portraying his character’s arrogance and impatience rather than just playing up his own comedic persona. Snipes complements Hart’s performance, and the two truly portray the complex dynamics of siblinghood. Of course, True Story relies on coincidences and occasionally stretches its premise beyond credibility. Even then, its fast-paced structure keeps the pressure building as the show moves between a thrilling crime story and an increasingly bitter family drama. COLLIDER . Collider · Quiz Collider Exclusive · Action Hero Quiz Which Action Hero Would Be Your Perfect Partner ? Rambo · James Bond · Indiana Jones · John McClane · Ethan Hunt Five legends. Five completely different ways of getting out alive — with style, with muscle, with charm, with luck, or with a plan so intricate it probably shouldn't work. Ten questions will reveal which action hero was built to have your back. 🎖️ Rambo 🍸 James Bond 🏺 Indiana Jones 🔧 John McClane 🎭 Ethan Hunt FIND YOUR PARTNER → QUESTION 1 / 10 THE MISSION 01 You're dropped into a dangerous situation with no warning. What do you need most from a partner? The first few seconds tell you everything about who belongs beside you. A Someone who already has three contingency plans running and is calmly working through all of them. B Someone who reads the terrain instinctively and knows exactly how to use it against the enemy. C Someone who keeps their nerve and their sense of humour when everything is falling apart. D Someone who knows the history of wherever we are and what we're walking into. E Someone with the right contact, the right cover identity, and the right exit already arranged. NEXT QUESTION → QUESTION 2 / 10 TRAVEL STYLE 02 You have to get somewhere dangerous, fast. How do you travel? How you get there is half the mission. A On foot through terrain no one else would attempt — I move where vehicles can't follow. B On a motorcycle, a cargo plane, or anything else that gets me there before I think too hard about it. C In something that belongs to someone else — borrowed, stolen, or improvised under fire. D First class, with a cover identity and a gadget that does something I won't explain until it's needed. E By whatever means are available — I've driven, flown, and once arrived by camel. The destination matters, not the method. NEXT QUESTION → QUESTION 3 / 10 UNDER FIRE 03 You're pinned down and outnumbered. What does your ideal partner do? This is when you find out what someone is really made of. A Disappears into the environment, flanks them silently, and ends it before I've reloaded. B Cracks a one-liner, grabs a fire extinguisher or a chair, and improvises something that somehow works. C Produces a gadget specifically designed for this exact scenario and uses it with infuriating precision. D Pulls out a whip, a pistol, and an archaeological insight that somehow gets us out alive. E Neutralises the threat with maximum efficiency and minimum words — they were already three moves ahead. NEXT QUESTION → QUESTION 4 / 10 DOWNTIME 04 The mission is paused. You have one evening to decompress. What does your partner suggest? Who someone is when the pressure drops is who they actually are. A A bar with terrible lighting, cold beer, and absolutely no questions about feelings. B The finest restaurant in the city, a bottle of something expensive, and a conversation that is equal parts brilliant and exhausting. C A local dig site, a museum after hours, or a long story about why that particular artefact matters to human civilisation. D Pizza. Bad TV. Falling asleep halfway through a movie neither of you were watching anyway. E A debrief that turns into three hours of contingency planning that somehow becomes the most fun you've had all week. NEXT QUESTION → QUESTION 5 / 10 COMMUNICATION 05 How do you prefer your partner to communicate mid-mission? Good communication is the difference between partners and a liability. A Precise and minimal — tell me what I need to know and nothing else. Every word has a cost. B Deadpan and dry — keeping it light keeps me sharp, even when everything is on fire. C Enthusiastic and slightly chaotic — but always with useful information buried somewhere in the noise. D Calm and controlled through an earpiece, with a plan that covers every variable I haven't thought of yet. E Barely at all — silence is a language and they speak it fluently. NEXT QUESTION → QUESTION 6 / 10 THE VILLAIN 06 Your enemy is powerful, well-resourced, and has the upper hand. How should your partner approach them? The approach to the enemy defines the partnership. A Infiltrate their inner circle, learn everything, and dismantle them from inside out before they know we're there. B Study the historical pattern — every villain of this type has a weakness written somewhere in the past. C Get them talking. The more they monologue, the more time I have to figure out how to beat them. D Go through them. Directly. With as much force as the terrain allows. E Find the one thing they haven't accounted for — there's always one thing — and make sure we're holding it. NEXT QUESTION → QUESTION 7 / 10 LOYALTY 07 Things go badly wrong and you're captured. What do you trust your partner to do? Who someone is when you need them most is the only thing that matters. A Come in alone, quietly, and get me out before anyone knows they were there. B Have already been working on the extraction since the moment I disappeared — the plan is already running. C Come in loud, come in fast, and worry about the collateral damage later — I'd do the same for them. D Use every resource, every contact, and bend every rule until I'm out — they don't leave people behind. E Charm their way in somehow, bluff through the hard part, and still manage to look good doing it. NEXT QUESTION → QUESTION 8 / 10 TOOLKIT 08 What does your ideal partner bring to the table that you couldn't replace? A great partner fills the gap you didn't know you had. A Technology that shouldn't exist yet and the training to use it under any conditions. B Survival instinct so refined it borders on supernatural — and the scars to prove it's been tested. C Knowledge of history, language, and culture that makes them invaluable in places where force is useless. D The ability to walk into any room in the world and immediately become the most trusted person in it. E Stubbornness that refuses to accept a situation is hopeless — and the improvisational skill to back it up. NEXT QUESTION → QUESTION 9 / 10 THE COST 09 Every partnership has a cost. Which of these can you live with? No one comes without baggage. The question is whether you can carry it together. A A partner who never fully switches off — always watching exits, always calculating threats, even at dinner. B A partner who gets the job done brilliantly but has the emotional availability of a locked filing cabinet. C A partner who makes everything ten times more complicated than it needs to be — but who always comes through. D A partner who gets personally attached to every relic, ruin, and artefact we encounter, which slows everything down. E A partner who was not built for this and knows it — but shows up anyway, every time, without being asked. NEXT QUESTION → QUESTION 10 / 10 THE LAST STAND 10 It's the final moment. Everything is on the line. What do you need from your partner right now? The last question is the most honest one. A One line. Absolutely dry. Delivered like the world isn't ending. Then we move. B Nothing said at all — just a look that means we both already know what has to happen. C A plan I don't fully understand that somehow accounts for everything, delivered in thirty seconds flat. D A piece of historical context that reframes the entire situation and tells us exactly what to do next. E Someone who steps forward instead of back — because that's who they've always been. REVEAL MY PARTNER → Your Partner Has Been Assigned Your Perfect Partner Is… Your answers have pointed to one action hero above all others. This is the person built to have your back — for better or considerably, spectacularly worse. YOUR PARTNER Rambo Your partner doesn't talk much, doesn't need to, and will have assessed every threat in your immediate environment before you've finished your first sentence. John Rambo is not a man of plans or politics — he is a force of nature shaped by survival, loyalty, and a capacity for endurance that goes beyond anything training can produce. He will not leave you behind. He has never left anyone behind who deserved to come home. What you get with Rambo is the most capable, most quietly ferocious partner imaginable — one who has been through things that would have broken anyone else, and who chose to keep going anyway. You'll never need to ask if he has your back. You'll just know. YOUR PARTNER James Bond Your partner will arrive perfectly dressed, perfectly briefed, and with a cover story so convincing it'll take you a moment to remember what's actually true. James Bond is the most professionally dangerous person in any room he enters — and the most disarmingly charming, which is the point. He operates in a world of layers, where nothing is what it appears and every advantage is used without apology. You'll never be bored. You'll occasionally be furious. But when it matters — when the mission is genuinely on the line and the margin for error has collapsed to nothing — Bond is exactly the partner you want. He has survived things that have no business being survivable. He does it with style. That is not nothing. YOUR PARTNER Indiana Jones Your partner will know the history, the language, the cultural context, and exactly why the thing everyone else is ignoring is actually the most important thing in the room. Indiana Jones is brilliant, reckless, and occasionally impossible — but he is also one of the most resourceful, most genuinely knowledgeable partners you could find yourself beside. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c4g7.text: Figure caption, Watch: There is ethnic cleansing in areas of the West Bank, says Miliband By Paul Adams ,Â Diplomatic correspondent Â and Â Henry Moore Published 8 September 2026, 18:09 BST Updated 1 hour ago The UK has announced sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, accusing Israel's government of turning a blind eye to the "ethnic cleansing" of Palestinians by settlers. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the move marked the "beginning of a new approach" to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, which "not only calls out injustice and suffering but acts". Israel's Foreign Minister Gideon Saar responded by accusing him of spreading an "outrageous lie" and announced counter-measures including shutting the UK's consulate in East Jerusalem. The UK sanctions will ban settlement goods but also act against companies and individuals providing services for settlement expansion. In West Bank, date farmers weigh impact of UK sanctions on Israeli settlers Published 5 hours ago How Israel is expanding settlements in drive to reshape West Bank Published 21 August The sanctions were launched alongside France and Canada, which in a joint statement with the UK said the action "marks a further turning point in our approach to protecting the two-state solution". Settlements are illegal under international law, and there has been a rise in violence towards Palestinians in the West Bank by settlers in recent months. In a statement to MPs, Miliband said: "The British government agrees that there is ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in areas of the West Bank, perpetrated by settler terrorists. "And all too often the Israeli government has turned a blind eye to this and worse, members of it have made statements and taken actions to support the forced displacement of Palestinians." He said ethnic cleansing was defined by the UN as a "purposeful policy designed by one ethnic or religious group to remove by violent means another ethnic or religious group from certain areas". Miliband said the official view of the government was that the Israeli occupation of the West Bank was unlawful because of the "entrenchment of its control, its intention to extend permanent sovereignty, and its expansionist agenda via illegal settlements". He said this position, which is in line with a 2024 advisory opinion from the International Court of Justice, should be reflected in the UK's "economic relationship" with the occupied West Bank. As a result, over the next six to nine months, the UK will introduce "a new comprehensive sanctions regime", he said. The foreign secretary also announced a ban on advertising illegal West Bank settlements in the UK. "The sanctions regime will target illegal settlements and settlement expansion, not Israel," Miliband added. Later on Tuesday, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the targeted measures were "aimed not at the Israeli people, but in support of the two-state solution". Announcing the closure of the consulate - which represents the UK government in Jerusalem, the West Bank and Gaza - Israel's Foreign Minister Saar said at a press conference: "We know that we have many friends in Britain. "Unfortunately, we have a hostile Labour government that is consistently operating against the State of Israel, and it has left us no choice but to respond to its hostile actions." He added that 11 UK MPs, including Jeremy Corbyn, Diane Abbott and all five sitting Green Party MPs, would be banned from entering Israel, accusing them of "antisemitic and anti-Israel activity". The UK also issued a joint statement with 11 other countries; France, Canada, Denmark, Spain, Finland, Ireland, Iceland, Norway, Poland, Portugal and Sweden. It said the group was unequivocally committed to the two-state solution and would introduce national measures or support European restrictions on trading goods with West Bank settlements. Image source, EPA Image caption, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband announced the measures on Tuesday The UK announcement comes after Israel opened up tenders for the construction of some 1,200 settlement homes in the so-called E1 area - a strategically important area east of Jerusalem. The plans have drawn widespread international condemnation. Israel has held off on plans to build in the area for decades under global pressure. Miliband told the Commons the UK's "new approach" was necessary because plans for the E1 development in the West Bank would render a two-state solution "unviable" by "cutting through the heart of Palestine". Elsewhere, he said the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, which triggered the Gaza war, carried "terrible echoes of the centuries of persecution of the Jewish people" and stressed Israel had "the right to protect its people and defend its territory". However, he added, "that cannot justify what has happened in Gaza". He said: "International humanitarian law imposes clear rules for states fighting wars, including to ensure access to food and medical supplies, to avoid mass displacement of civilians, and to avoid the targeting of civilians. Serious and international violations of this law, if proven, amount to war crimes. "What has occurred, including the actions of the IDF (Israel Defense Forces), have been examined in depth by a number of organisations, including the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry. "The conclusions of these reports represent increasing evidence that war crimes appear to have been committed, and we support legal processes to determine this." He added it was up to international courts to determine if Israel had committed genocide in Gaza. Israel's leaders have consistently rejected allegations of genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes. They have insisted that Israeli forces have operated in accordance with international law. Figure caption, Why is the UK against Israel's proposed West Bank E1 settlement? Miliband began his statement to the Commons by referring to his Jewish roots and childhood experiences of visiting Israel, as well as recent antisemitic attacks in the UK. He described himself as "a proud British Jew" and outlined his steadfast support for the state of Israel. He said: "My personal story and that of thousands of British Jews is one of the many reasons why I say to anyone here or around the world who questions Israel's right to exist as a homeland for the Jewish people - you are wrong, and we will call you out whenever you engage in this attempt at the erasure of Israel." But the UK's Chief Rabbi Sir Ephraim Mirvis said it was a "truly a dark day for British Jews", saying the sanctions were "little more than political flag bearing for mendacious anti-Israel rhetoric" that would embolden people who "use hatred as a weapon against Jews". The Board of Deputies of British Jews expressed "deep regret" over Tuesday's announcement, and urged both the UK and Israeli governments to "avoid pursuing what appear to be party interests over national interests". Responding in the Commons, Conservative shadow foreign secretary Tom Tugendhat claimed ministers were "enacting policies that the Foreign Office knows won't work". He agreed that illegal settlements were wrong and "some Israeli ministers have indulged in hateful propaganda and incitement" but added "this isn't about Israel alone and it certainly isn't about reducing the complexity of the region to a single sentence. Sadly, the government is in the process of doing just that". Israel's foreign minister Saar said on Tuesday evening he had spoken with Tugendhat and Tory leader Kemi Badenoch, thanking them "for their firm opposition to the hostile Labour government's announcement today and its series of anti-Israel policies since taking office". He also said British representatives from the International Gaza Support Center in Kiryat Gat in southern Israel would be removed, and UK activities to train Palestinian Authority forces in Judea and Samaria - how the Israeli government refers to the West Bank - would be terminated. Speaking earlier on Tuesday, the country's President Isaac Herzog said the decision would "fall on the wrong side of history", adding: "In the current context, it would be a gross interference in the democratic elections of a sovereign nation." Herzog said the move would directly harm Palestinians and urged foreign governments to turn towards "constructive dialogue" and cooperation, adding "sanctions are not a solution". US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters the White House had no comment on the joint action, adding that "obviously we're not going to do what the UK did". Earlier, Donald Trump's ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee earlier told the BBC that the US - Israel's most powerful ally - would "without a doubt" respond to the expected sanctions, warning of a "huge economic impact on British businesses". He suggested action could be taken by individual US states as well as at a central, federal level. The Palestinian presidency welcomed the UK's decision, saying it was "an important step towards confronting Israel's colonial system and its violations against the Palestinian people". As part of the UK announcement, Miliband also announced sanctions on the financing wing of Lebanon's Hezbollah, the Iran-backed armed group. New sanctions in line with the US and European Union were also announced on Iran. The intervention comes almost a year after Sir Keir Starmer's government recognised a state of Palestine, and said the UK had a moral responsibility to support a peaceful future for Israelis and Palestinians. Israel rejects a two-state solution. It says any final settlement must be the result of negotiations with the Palestinians, and statehood should not be a precondition. The Palestinian Authority backs a two-state solution but Palestinian armed group Hamas does not because it is opposed to the existence of Israel. Hamas says that it could accept an interim Palestinian state based on 1967 de facto borders, without officially recognising Israel, if refugees were given the right to return. Israel has built about 160 settlements housing 700,000 Jews since it occupied the West Bank and East Jerusalem during the 1967 Middle East war. An estimated 3.3 million Palestinians live alongside them. There has been a surge in attacks by settlers on Palestinians and their property in the West Bank since the start of the Gaza war, which was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023. https://www.politico.eu/article/les-renf.text: BRUXELLES — Alors que l’UE prévoit de renforcer les moyens d’Europol à l’ère de l’intelligence artificielle, de hauts responsables européens mettent en garde que cela ne doit pas se faire au détriment de la protection de la vie privée des Européens. Face aux cybercriminels, terroristes et espions qui se servent de l’intelligence artificielle pour faire des escroqueries, de l’extorsion et des cyberattaques, Bruxelles mise sur le renforcement des compétences en matière d’IA d’Europol — l’agence qui coordonne les renseignements policiers européens depuis 1998 — afin de lutter contre ces menaces. “Europol est à un tournant”, a énoncé Fabienne Keller, députée européenne Renew membre de la commission des Libertés civiles. “Nous avons besoin d’un Europol plus fort, doté des ressources et des capacités nécessaires pour soutenir efficacement les forces de l’ordre nationales”, a-t-elle plaidé. Cela “doit aller de pair avec un fort contrôle démocratique et des garde-fous solides en matière de droits fondamentaux et de protection des données”. Advertisement Advertisement L’UE a dévoilé cet été un projet visant à opérer une “évolution transformatrice” de l’agence basée à La Haye. Il est question de doubler son budget pour le porter à 3 milliards d’euros, et de lui conférer un rôle actif dans la lutte contre les nouvelles menaces, en lui donnant accès à davantage de données et à des technologies de pointe. Alors que les développeurs et les responsables politiques débattent de l’opportunité de ralentir le développement des modèles d’IA de pointe , les forces de l’ordre, elles, sont déjà confrontées à des criminels qui utilisent les technologies les plus récentes. Mais ce projet soulève aussi des questions en matière de gouvernance et protection de la vie privée, suscitant un débat houleux sur l’étendue des pouvoirs dont devraient disposer les forces de l’ordre pour assurer la sécurité des citoyens face à l’IA et grâce à celle-ci. Wojciech Wiewiórowski, le Contrôleur européen de la protection des données (CEPD), qui veille à ce que l’ensemble des agences et institutions de l’UE respectent les règles en la matière, s’est dit “tout à fait favorable” à l’idée de donner à Europol les moyens d’utiliser des données et de nouveaux outils basés sur l’intelligence artificielle. Mais il “faut qu’il y ait un contrôle”, a-t-il ajouté. “Quand j’entends parler du renforcement d’Europol, de la modification de son champ d’action et d’investissements vraiment très importants dans l’agence elle-même, je m’en réjouis en tant que citoyen”, a-t-il poursuivi. “Mais je me dois de poser la question : pourquoi il n’y a rien dans la proposition sur la manière de superviser Europol ?” Plus rapide et à grande échelle Pour Jürgen Ebner, directeur général adjoint de l’agence, qui a été nommé le mois dernier à sa tête, la lutte contre la criminalité exige aujourd’hui de doter Europol de toutes les capacités offertes par l’intelligence artificielle. Advertisement Advertisement “L’IA transforme la manière dont les crimes sont commis dans un large éventail d’activités criminelles”, a-t-il exposé une semaine après avoir été désigné par les représentants des Etats membres pour occuper ce poste , sous réserve de l’avis du Parlement européen. “L’IA rend les activités criminelles plus rapides, plus sophistiquées et plus faciles à mener à grande échelle. Cela représente un défi de taille pour les forces de l’ordre.” Europol, qui emploie plus de 1 700 personnes, a été conçu comme une organisation de centralisation, collaborant avec les services de police européens afin de faciliter l’analyse et le partage d’éventuels éléments de preuve et d’autres informations liées aux enquêtes criminelles. Dans le cadre du nouveau projet, l’UE compte désormais sur cette agence pour mettre au point de nouvelles façons d’utiliser l’IA afin de passer au crible les montagnes de données disponibles et d’aider les forces de police nationales à résoudre des affaires en temps réel. Jürgen Ebner, directeur général adjoint d’Europol, qui a été nommé le mois dernier à la tête de l’agence, s’exprime lors d’une conférence de presse à Bruxelles, le 26 juin 2026. | Olivier Hoslet/EPA Si les plus récentes avancées en matière d’intelligence artificielle peuvent être utiles aux criminels comme aux forces de l’ordre, ces dernières doivent en plus respecter les principes démocratiques. Alors qu’Europol pourra traiter un volume d’informations potentiellement colossal, la protection de la vie privée pourrait bien être le principe le plus menacé. Cet enjeu est au cœur des préoccupations de Jürgen Ebner, qui est désormais pratiquement assuré de diriger Europol pendant les quatre prochaines années. Il a pointé les contrôles juridiques qui pèsent sur les forces de police lorsqu’elles tentent d’utiliser l’IA. Pour lui, l’accès rapide aux preuves électroniques est essentiel pour tirer le meilleur parti des capacités émergentes de l’intelligence artificielle. “Elle peut aider les enquêteurs à filtrer de grands volumes de preuves numériques, à relier des informations entre elles et à identifier des renseignements exploitables”, a détaillé l’Allemand. “L’IA peut démultiplier les capacités des enquêteurs et des analystes, et leur donner davantage de temps pour interpréter les preuves.” Advertisement Advertisement Vie privée versus sécurité Les débats sur la manière dont la police collecte et traite les données des citoyens opposent souvent la sécurité à la vie privée. Toutefois, Jürgen Ebner a argué devant les policiers, lors d’une conférence à Lisbonne le mois dernier, qu’Europol ne devait pas basculer dans une situation où “la collecte de données devient une fin en soi, la technologie sert à justifier son propre usage, ou l’urgence sert de prétexte pour abandonner les garde-fous”. S’également aux forces de police de toute l’Europe réunies à Lisbonne, Wojciech Wiewiórowski, le Contrôleur européen de la protection des données, a considéré que la proposition de l’UE “jette officiellement les bases d’une action policière en Europe fondée sur l’intelligence artificielle et les données”. Le CEPD avait déjà épinglé Europol au sujet de ses pratiques en matière de collecte de données et s’était opposé à une proposition antérieure visant à élargir le champ de compétence de l’agence. Il a averti que la proposition de réforme d’Europol comportait de graves risques en matière de vie privée , et permettrait à l’agence de conserver des données sur un “vaste” nombre de personnes n’ayant aucun lien avec des activités criminelles “pendant une période prolongée et indéterminée”. La proposition préserve, certes, le rôle du CEPD dans la supervision d’Europol, mais Wojciech Wiewiórowski a pointé qu’elle ne prévoyait pas, parallèlement à l’expansion d’Europol, un renforcement équivalent des pouvoirs ou des ressources du CEPD. Il a également jugé qu’elle accordait “trop de pouvoirs aux organes internes d’Europol, sans contrôle extérieur”. Pour le délégué à la protection des données d’Europol, Daniel Drewer, ces mesures accélérées sont nécessaires dans un monde marqué par “une évolution technologique rapide qui ne profite pas uniquement aux forces de police ou aux acteurs étatiques, mais également aux réseaux criminels”. Advertisement Advertisement La réforme d’Europol intervient alors que le CEPD peine déjà à faire face à ses nouvelles responsabilités en matière de contrôle de l’utilisation de l’IA par les institutions européennes. Par ailleurs, Stéphane Duguin, un ancien responsable de la lutte contre la cybercriminalité chez Europol et aujourd’hui à la tête de Protect.ngo, affirme que les forces de l’ordre ont également du mal à suivre le rythme des avancées technologiques et stratégiques de leurs adversaires. Au-delà des défis liés à leurs capacités techniques, il estime que le réseau policier européen doit également surmonter les obstacles liés à sa structure, mise en place il y a longtemps. Les criminels ne commettent “pas seulement des cybercrimes, de s’ingérer dans les affaires étrangères ou de manipuler l’information, mais c’est ainsi que fonctionnent les forces de police. Et c’est là le problème”, souligne Stéphane Duguin. “Si l’on considère Europol hors de son contexte, cela n’a aucun sens, car c’est l’ensemble de la chaîne judiciaire qui doit évoluer. Si l’on dispose de moyens accrus pour enquêter sur les crimes en ligne mais qu’à la fin, les affaires ne sont pas portées devant les tribunaux en raison de la législation nationale, alors cela n’a aucun sens.” Cet article a d’abord été publié par POLITICO en anglais, puis a été édité en français par Jean-Christophe Catalon.

https://business-review.eu/business/huma.text: PwC survey: Fear of job cuts and political decisions among workers in Romania “The results need to be read in the economic context in which they were collected. Romania entered 2026 with the highest inflation rate in the European Union, and the effect shows directly in household budgets. The good news is that, in a difficult year, motivation has risen rather than fallen, and the intention to change employer has declined. Workers are willing to stay and do more, but they need trust and support from managers who explain and coordinate change. For employers, the message is clear: the workforce is motivated and adaptable enough, but it needs to be mobilised through a clear, coherent and well-communicated vision in order to have a visible impact on transformation,” said Oana Munteanu, Director and Workforce Leader, PwC Romania . Almost six in ten respondents (58%) say they pay their bills with little or nothing left over at the end of the month, compared with 50% in 2025 and 52% in the region, while the share struggling to pay their bills has risen from 10% to 17%, close to the regional average. Among workers affected at work by the rising cost of living, 46% say it has increased their stress levels, compared with 34% in the region. Over the past year, the rising cost of living had the strongest impact, with 71% of workers in Romania reporting a moderate or major impact at work, compared with 56% in the region. It was followed by domestic political decisions (62% vs. 49%), concern about job cuts (61% vs. 50%) and geopolitical conflict (59% vs. 48%). On each of these pressures, Romania records the highest level among the countries analysed. Over the next three years, the main perceived threats to job security are economic volatility, conflicts between countries, AI taking on more tasks and companies relocating work to lower-cost locations. At the same time, confidence in job security has fallen, as has the intention to change employer. The share of workers who are very or extremely confident in their job security fell from 58% in 2025 to 48% in 2026, and the share who say they are very or extremely likely to change employer in the next 12 months fell from 25% to 18%. Motivation, however, remains high: 73% of workers feel proud of their work at least once a week, compared with a regional average of 64%. In addition, 65% are willing to go above and beyond at least once a week, up from 57% in 2025. Read more about Romania delivered more than 636,000 new homes over the past decade read more Pay and stability are the top priorities At the same time, 37% of workers say they are very or extremely likely to ask for a pay raise in the next 12 months, and 32% say the same about a promotion. As in previous years, pay and benefits remain the number one priority when workers assess their job, cited among their top three priorities by 65%, followed by job security (53%). Overall, 42% of respondents feel they are paid fairly relative to the value they contribute. Six in ten workers in Romania (61%) would not accept lower pay or benefits, 47% would not accept less job security and 44% would not accept longer hours or a faster pace of work, while a negative work culture is a dealbreaker for 34%, compared with 50% globally. PwC’s Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2026 was conducted in May and June 2026 among 49,364 workers across 48 countries and regions, including 447 in Romania. Regional comparisons cover Romania, Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary. The full report is available here .
